title: I am a former food expert from the USDA: this is how to avoid stomach beds when eating on vacation and sailing as the virus increases.
text:
Thousands of people are victims of the unpleasant stomach insects on vacation every year, and this week, there was a viral outbreak on a Cruise in Florida.
And although a stomach virus is the last thing anyone wants on vacation, forced to spend their days out of noise on a bathroom, a food security expert told Dailymail.com that it could be the reality for thousands of people who escape In the ships.
Dr. Darin Detwiler, a former Food Expert from USDA, told the Dailymail.com virus like E.Coli, Salmonella and Norovirus are common on the cruises due to narrow neighborhoods, thousands of people on board and the high volume of communal foods.
Highly contagious infections spread through contaminated foods, water or inappropriate food handling, and cause abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, chills and fatigue.
In severe cases, patients can dehydrate or enter into organic failure and need to be hospitalized.
This week, the CDC reported 107 passengers and 12 crew members aboard Mrs. Rotterdam of the Holland America line, which left out of Port Everglades, Florida, on February 2, has hired Norovirus.
Norovirus is highly contagious and is the main cause of vomiting and diarrhea and in the United States, according to CDC.
The Vessel (VSP) sanitation program of the CDC traces and inspects outbreaks of cruise gastrointestinal diseases and has registered seven this year, affecting approximately 700 people. In 2024, the agency registered 18 incidents, affecting more than 1,000 people.
Dr. Darin Detwiler, an outstanding food security expert in the United States, told Dailymail.com Norovirus is the most common gastrographic disease on the high seas
Of those outbreaks, most were caused by Norovirus, but Salmonella and E. coli were behind several.
These viruses are commonly caused by the ingestion of water or foods that have been contaminated with feces, or consuming little cooked foods, such as meat, eggs or fish. Viruses can spread when someone comes into contact with an infected person or a surface that a sick person has touched.
In general, CDC estimates between two and four percent of cruise passengers experience these diseases every year.
And with an estimate of 31.7 million people who sail worldwide, more than 500,000 could get sick.
Cruises face ‘unique challenges’ when it comes to food security, says Dr. Detwiler’, particularly because they serve a large number of passengers in closed spaces where diseases can spread rapidly. They are like floating cities.
He added: ‘Cruises also generally obtain foods internationally, stopping in several ports to replace supplies. This can result in different safety standards, especially when it comes to fresh products, meats and seafood.
While most gastrointestinal diseases imply mild symptoms, vulnerable populations, such as young children, older people and pregnant women, can face more serious complications such as severe dehydration, organic insufficiency, ‘or in extreme cases, death’.
To reduce the possibilities of getting sick while he was at sea, the university professor told this website his seven security measures.
Wash your hands often the outdated form

The most effective way to prevent cruise infections, said Dr. Detwiler, is to wash your hands with soap and water regularly for 20 seconds, or the duration of two happy birthday songs.
He pointed out that this is something particularly important before meals.
While alcohol -based disinfectants are “useful”, these can be “less effective against Norovirus, so it prioritizes hands washing.”
In an attempt to put young children with the habit of washing their hands, Dr. Detwiler recommended educating them around stomach insects and the possibility of getting sick.
Avoid buffet at peak hours Dr. Detwiler advises dinner during the lowest activity when the food rotation in the buffet is higher or opts for articles made to request
It is known that buffets are critical points for pollution, especially when food is left out for long periods.
To minimize the risk, Dr. Detwiler advises dinner during the least activity hours, when food billing is greater or opts for articles made to request. ”
During peak hours, there is a higher risk of pollution since people pile up at food stations.
CDC stress that hot food should be ‘smoking’, while cold food must be visibly cold.
The agency said: “The germs that cause food poisoning grow rapidly when the food is in the danger zone, between 40 degrees Fahrenheit and 140 degrees Fahrenheit.”
These temperatures allow bacteria to multiply more quickly, with the germs Norovirus and E. coli that flourish.
Norovirus is the most common type of stomach insect and usually occurs when a sick person touches food before serving it. However, foods such as fish and shellfish can naturally contaminate it.
While most people recover without complications, serious vomiting and diarrhea can lead to dehydration, which requires medical care.
E.Coli is a bacterium that causes similar symptoms. It can also be in raw and little cooked meats. Most strains are soft, but some can cause severe cramps and bloody dialycies.
Note how food is being prepared While visiting buffet stations on the ship or other dining areas, Dr. Detwiler told Dailymail.com that it is important to see how food and drinks are prepared.
Some of their bulletins are servers that do not wear gloves, which serve spoons and food stored at wrong temperatures.
Meanwhile, in cruise bars, he said that beverage garrisons should be avoided.
A 2007 study published in the Journal of Environmental Health found that almost 70 percent of lemon slices used as bars garnishes were contaminated with bacteria.
Dr. Detwiler says that if you see unhealthy activities while sailing, “it is very important to speak and say something.”
Omits oysters and steak tartar “Raw seafood and little cooked meats, such as fillet tartar or cooked chuletones, are more likely to transport pathogens,” said Dr. Detwiler
While raw bars, supplied with everything, from oysters to clams, are considered an extravagant dining option in the sea, Dr. Detwiler advises staying away from them.
In fact, he recommends omitting raw or little cooked foods together due to possible pollution.
He explained: ‘raw shellfish and little cooked meats, such as fillet tartar or rare cooked chuletones, are more likely to transport pathogens. You even run a risk with liquid eggs.
“Opt for well -cooked dishes to reduce the risk of exposure to Salmonella or Listeria.”
People with Salmonella develop stomach problems and fever, which can become severe and require hospitalization.
Many of these foods can also house Listeria, which is Usually, it is found in non -pasteurized milk, soft cheeses, food ready for eating, fish, cured meats and preorted fruits.
Most people with Listeria will not fall seriously ill. But in some cases, it can cause confusion and seizures, spontaneous abortion in pregnant women and even death.
Adhere to bottled water and be careful with the ice Although cruises purify their water, Dr. Detwiler said that bottled water is a “much safer option and is worth paying a little more.”
This is because the cruise water could be contaminated with Escherichia Enterotoxigenic (ETEC), a type of E. coli bacteria that can cause diarrhea. It can also be the source of Legionella, a bacterium that can cause legionaries’ disease.
Legionnaires is a serious type of pneumonia that can cause lack of breath, as well as gastrointestinal symptoms. About 10 percent of people who contract the disease die.
For this reason, you should also consider the search for ice in your drinks if you can, said Dr. Detwiler to Dailymail.com.
He added: “Be careful with drinking tap water or using ice, particularly when attached to foreign ports where water quality can vary.”
Short and peel your own fruit Instead of cutting fruits, Dr. Detwiler recommends selecting entire fruits from the dining areas and ‘cut it or peel it to avoid pollution’
While melon slices and pieces of pineapple may seem attractive in buffet counters, Dr. Detwiler reveals that “pre -cut fruits entail the risk of being exposed to bacteria.”
In recent years there have been several outbreaks of bacteria linked to fruit. More recently, in 2023, there was a national outbreak of Salmonella linked to Cantaloupes, with 407 sick people and six deaths.
For this reason, Dr. Detwiler says that “he will always avoid the melon due to the frequency with which diseases and deaths are contaminated and causes.”
Instead of cutting fruits, recommend selecting entire fruits from the dining areas and ‘cut it or peel it to avoid pollution’.
Jump street food on land The risk of stomach diseases in cruises extends beyond the ship.
Most cruise companies offer excursions on land, where tourists leave the ship and explore an area for the day, giving people the opportunity to try the local cuisine.
But Dr. Detwiler warned of street food, especially when high temperatures can serve as a culture broth for harmful bacteria.
He says: ‘When exploring in Port Stops, consider food safety standards in local markets.
“Sing in restaurants of good reputation and avoid street food that may not meet the same levels of hygiene as the cruise.”
